item.title: Man Utd debt remains above FJ$3B, with FJ$188M spent on land for new stadium

item.content:encoded:
Manchester United's overall debt remains above £1 billion, which is about FJ$3 billion, despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5 million, which is about FJ$188 million, buying land for its new stadium.

Amid fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, the club has announced record revenues of £677.6 million, which is about FJ$2.01 billion, and an operating profit of £22.6 million, which is about FJ$67 million, despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.

United also confirmed it spent £63.5 million, or about FJ$188 million, of an additional US$125 million, equivalent to £94.14 million or about FJ$279 million, added to its historic debt during a summer refinancing move, on land for its new stadium.

The club has not explained what it has done with the remainder.

The stadium itself is likely to cost more than £2 billion, which is about FJ$5.93 billion.

This comes at a time when supporters are frustrated over what they believe was a lack of sufficient investment in Michael Carrick's first-team squad this summer.

United spent £148 million, which is about FJ$439 million, on three new signings, Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, this summer.

This was less than a third of the £458 million, or about FJ$1.36 billion, Manchester City invested in its squad and was even lower than the amount spent by newly promoted Ipswich.

However, fans are unhappy that an additional left-back was not purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has already missed three matches through injury, or that further striking support was not brought in for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season while recovering from a shin complaint that has since resurfaced.

While United says the additional funds were earmarked for its new stadium, which is planned to be built 350 yards from the current Old Trafford, the loan itself is lodged within the club's accounts.

NZ Rugby weighs Super Rugby Pacific exit as financial pressure mounts

item.content:encoded:
The uncertainty surrounding the long-term future of Super Rugby Pacific has grown further ahead of a key meeting tomorrow, following a report that New Zealand Rugby (NZR) will discuss the possibility of abandoning the competition altogether.

According to The Post , one of three proposals to be discussed at NZR’s summit tomorrow is the creation of a domestic competition involving 8 to 10 New Zealand teams, replacing both the NPC and Super Rugby.

With financial losses continuing to eat into the cash injection provided through the Silver Lake private equity deal in 2022, the summit will bring together stakeholders from across the game.

The powerful provincial unions are reportedly leading the push to move away from Super Rugby.

A leaked document titled Rugby System Programme – Rugby Summit Pre-read last week revealed the extent of NZR’s financial difficulties, including a projected cumulative loss of NZ$108 million between 2024 and 2028.

The document also showed that NZR generated record revenue of NZ$285 million in 2025 but still recorded a loss of NZ$19 million.

More significantly, only two of New Zealand’s five Super Rugby franchises have made a profit in any year between 2019 and 2025 without financial support from NZR.

However, there are reportedly two other options being considered.

One would involve adding two more teams to Super Rugby, which is set to contract to just 10 sides in 2027 following the departure of Moana Pasifika.

The other would be to consolidate the Super Rugby and NPC organisations into the home cities of the five existing New Zealand franchises.

The NPC has been at the heart of New Zealand rugby for decades and remains an important part of the country’s player development pathway.

It is also one of the main reasons NZR has resisted calls for a global rugby season, which would move The Rugby Championship from its current August–October window to February–April.

A key question for tomorrow’s discussions will be whether an 8 to a 10-team competition based on the NPC model could generate enough revenue, and, more importantly, make a profit while also meeting NZR’s high-performance objectives.
